title: SME Growth Fund: Cabinet clears ₹10,000 crore equity fund for SMEs
excerpt: The Cabinet approved a ₹10,000 crore SME Growth Fund on 6 October 2026. What it funds, who may qualify, how it works and what it means for Indian startups.
content:
On 6 October 2026 India's Union Cabinet approved a ₹10,000 crore government commitment to a new SME Growth Fund. The fund will buy equity stakes directly in small and medium enterprises (SMEs) that have outgrown early-stage money but cannot yet raise large private equity, according to the Press Information Bureau (PIB). (One crore is 10 million, so ₹10,000 crore is ₹100 billion.) Most of the money is meant for manufacturers, including firms in industrial clusters in smaller cities. The rules on who qualifies and how to apply have not been published yet.

Key takeaways

  • The Cabinet approved the government's ₹10,000 crore commitment to the SME Growth Fund (SGF), first announced in the Union Budget 2026-27 on 1 February.
  • The money goes into an Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) set up under the SGF framework. It will take equity stakes, not make loans.
  • The majority is earmarked for small and medium manufacturing enterprises. SMEs in industrial clusters in Tier-II and Tier-III cities will also be considered.
  • Eligibility criteria, ticket sizes, the fund manager and the application process have not been announced.
  • For most early-stage startups this is not new money. It is aimed at businesses that already have proven operations and need capital to scale.

What the Cabinet approved

The PIB release, issued by the Ministry of Finance at 3:14 pm on 6 October, says the Cabinet chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi approved the government's commitment of ₹10,000 crore towards setting up the SGF. The fund covers manufacturing, services, technology, innovation-driven sectors and "strategic value chains". It puts into effect paragraph 28 of the Budget 2026-27 speech.

The release describes the problem the fund is meant to solve. Existing equity funds mostly back early-stage companies, and mostly micro enterprises. That leaves what the government calls a structural gap in growth capital for small and medium firms. Credit schemes have made loans easier to get, the release says. What is still missing is long-term risk capital for businesses that want to scale up, adopt new technology, expand abroad or buy other companies.

Electronics and IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw briefed reporters on the Cabinet decisions, Deccan Chronicle reported. The public broadcaster's DD India reported the same focus on growth-stage SMEs with demonstrated viability.

How the fund is meant to work

The government will make an "aggregate commitment" of ₹10,000 crore to an AIF set up under the SGF framework, the PIB release says. An AIF is a pooled investment fund, the structure Indian venture capital and private equity funds commonly use. So the government is acting as an investor in a fund, and that fund will take minority or growth stakes in companies. It is not a grant or a subsidised loan scheme.

The release calls this "patient growth equity capital" for high-potential SMEs with proven viability and scalability. That points to businesses with revenue, operating history and a credible expansion plan, not idea-stage startups. Business Standard described the target as businesses with established operations and the potential to scale.

The release does not say who will manage the fund, how large a single investment can be, how long the fund will run or how it will exit its stakes. It also does not say whether private investors will be asked to invest alongside the government. SMEStreet and CorpLawUpdates both flagged these as open questions. Any figure you see for ticket sizes or matching capital is, for now, someone's estimate.

Who could qualify

The official release gives the fund's priorities, not a formal eligibility test:

  • Size: small and medium enterprises. The release says micro enterprises are already served by existing equity funds.
  • Sector: a majority of the money goes to manufacturing-focused SMEs. Services, technology and innovation-led businesses are also in scope.
  • Location: SMEs in industrial clusters in Tier-II and Tier-III cities will be considered.
  • Stage: businesses at a turning point, such as adding capacity, adopting technology, entering export markets, joining global supply chains or making acquisitions.

The release does not say which definition of "small" and "medium" applies. The current legal definitions came into force on 1 April 2025 through notification S.O. 1364(E), according to Taxmann:

CategoryInvestment in plant, machinery or equipmentAnnual turnover
MicroUp to ₹2.5 croreUp to ₹10 crore
SmallUp to ₹25 croreUp to ₹100 crore
MediumUp to ₹125 croreUp to ₹500 crore

If the fund follows these limits, a business with ₹10–500 crore in turnover would be in its range. That is our reading, not an official rule. Wait for the operating guidelines.

Where the fund fits in the Budget's MSME plan

The SGF is one part of a three-part approach in the Budget: equity, liquidity and professional support. A PIB backgrounder dated 15 February 2026 sets it out:

  • Equity: the ₹10,000 crore SGF, plus ₹2,000 crore more for the Self-Reliant India (SRI) Fund. The SRI Fund was set up in 2021 to keep risk capital flowing to micro enterprises. As of 30 November 2025 it had invested ₹15,442 crore in 682 MSMEs.
  • Liquidity: changes to TReDS, the government-backed online platform where MSMEs sell their unpaid invoices to financiers. More than ₹7 lakh crore has already been made available to MSMEs through it.
  • Professional support: a cadre of trained "Corporate Mitras" in Tier-II and Tier-III towns to help small firms meet compliance requirements at lower cost.

The TReDS plan has four measures, Outlook Business reported. TReDS becomes the settlement platform for purchases by central public-sector companies from MSMEs. Credit guarantees through CGTMSE will cover invoice discounting. The GeM procurement portal will be linked with TReDS, and TReDS receivables can be turned into asset-backed securities. The Budget also proposed reviving 200 legacy industrial clusters.

The scale of the sector explains the focus. According to the PIB backgrounder, MSMEs account for about 35.4% of India's manufacturing, 48.58% of exports and 31.1% of GDP. More than 7.47 crore enterprises employ over 32.82 crore people.

How far ₹10,000 crore goes

The amount is large for a government equity programme but small next to the size of the sector. Rakesh Chhabra, president of the Federation of Indian Micro and Small & Medium Enterprises (FISME), gave Business Standard a rough illustration. At an average investment of ₹10 crore, the fund would cover about 1,000 enterprises, before fees, expenses and money held back for follow-on rounds. He stressed that this was not a forecast. His point was that bringing in private capital, and getting SMEs ready for equity investors, will decide the impact.

Getting ready for equity is a real hurdle. Taking an outside shareholder means audited accounts, a clean cap table, board oversight and regular reporting. Many family-run manufacturers have never needed these. Shrikant Goyal, managing director of Getfive Funds, told Business Standard the fund could improve governance and reporting standards. It could also give private funds a pipeline of businesses ready for institutional investors.

Not everyone expects the benefits to spread widely. SMEStreet quoted A Vikram Joshe, founder of WAE Ltd, who said the gains will go mostly to formal businesses that are ready to grow, not to MSMEs across the board.

What it means for Indian startups

Hardware and manufacturing startups past Series A gain the most. A company making EV components, electronics, speciality chemicals or industrial equipment, with ₹50–300 crore in revenue, falls in the gap the government describes. It is too large for seed funds and often too asset-heavy or slow-growing for typical venture capital. If it is registered as an MSME, the SGF may become a new source of growth equity.

Software and consumer startups are less likely to be the main target, since most of the money is earmarked for manufacturing. The release does keep services, technology and innovation-led sectors in scope.

Early-stage founders should not expect much from this fund. The government says the gap it is filling is at the growth stage, not the start.

What to do now: make sure your Udyam registration is current, keep audited financials for at least three years, and get your cap table and governance into a state an institutional investor would accept. Then watch for the fund's operating guidelines. This article is general information, not investment or legal advice. Confirm details with official notifications or a qualified adviser before acting.

Why it matters

India has built strong credit support for MSMEs through guarantees, TReDS and priority-sector lending. But it has had little growth equity for firms between micro and mid-sized. The SGF is the government's first large, dedicated attempt to fill that gap with equity rather than debt. Whether it works depends on details not yet published: who runs the fund, how fast it invests, and whether private capital comes in alongside it. We will update this piece when the guidelines are out. Meanwhile, you can follow Indian funding rounds on our funding tracker and policy news in our news section.

Frequently asked questions

What is the SME Growth Fund?

A government-backed equity fund for small and medium enterprises. The Cabinet approved a ₹10,000 crore government commitment to it on 6 October 2026. It will be set up as an Alternative Investment Fund and will take equity stakes in high-potential SMEs.

Is the SME Growth Fund a loan scheme?

No. It provides equity, meaning ownership stakes, not loans or subsidies. The government says this is to fill a gap in long-term risk capital that credit schemes do not cover.

Which businesses will it fund?

Mainly small and medium manufacturing enterprises with proven, scalable businesses, including those in Tier-II and Tier-III industrial clusters. Services, technology and innovation-led SMEs are also in scope. Detailed eligibility criteria have not been published.

How can an SME apply?

There is no application process yet. The Cabinet approval did not name a fund manager or set out how to apply. Watch for official guidelines from the Ministry of Finance or the Ministry of MSME.

Can micro enterprises get money from it?

The fund is aimed at small and medium firms. Micro enterprises are covered by other schemes, including the Self-Reliant India Fund, which the Budget topped up with ₹2,000 crore.

When was the fund announced?

It was announced in the Union Budget 2026-27 on 1 February 2026 and approved by the Cabinet on 6 October 2026.
